title: How To Build Rapport With A Mask On
author: Michael Linsin
summary: With masks and social distancing removing a teacher's smile and physical closeness, Linsin offers four substitute tools for building rapport: exaggerated eye contact that still conveys a smile, a distance-friendly 'air bump' gesture of acknowledgment, deliberately expressive hand gestures to replace facial cues, and a cut in overall talking time paired with clearer, more deliberate speech. He cites the statistic that most communication is nonverbal to justify leaning harder on gesture and tone once the lower half of the face is hidden. The piece frames these workarounds not as a lesser substitute but as evidence that good teachers find a way regardless of circumstance, closing with the hope that these adaptations will make everyone better communicators once masks are no longer necessary.
points: Strong, held eye contact combined with an exaggerated eye-crinkle is offered as a mask-compatible substitute for a visible smile.
A hands-free 'air bump' — fist out from the shoulder after eye contact — replaces physical contact as a quick acknowledgment gesture.
Deliberately expressive hand gestures are recommended to make up for the loss of facial expression under a mask.
Cutting overall talking time by roughly a third to a half, while speaking more clearly and pausing more, improves attentiveness.
The four tools are framed as more than sufficient workarounds, since good teachers find a way around any circumstance.
quotes: No longer can you rely on your smile to express warmth, enthusiasm, and pride in your students. A single look that once spoke more than a thousand words has been taken away.
An important key is to first hold their eye contact for a beat. Wait until you’re locked in, then smile and let your creases show.
You’ve heard that 93 percent of communication is nonverbal. If you take away the bottom half of your face, then you absolutely must start using your hands to make up the difference.
Here at SCM, we recommend cutting the amount of talking you normally do by one-third to one-half. You should see dramatic results.
Good teachers, however, find a way. We accept the challenge. We look plainly and honestly at what is in front of us and find a workaround.
But in the long run, when we’re finally beyond masks and social distancing, we’ll all be better communicators, rapport-builders, and teachers.
